title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper argues that the rapid spread of generative AI in education, especially ChatGPT and other large language models, requires schools to rethink how students and teachers use these tools. The central problem is not whether AI should be present in classrooms, but how institutions can avoid misuse, overreliance, hallucinations, unfair advantages, and loss of independent thinking while still taking advantage of AI’s potential for personalized learning and support.

The article proposes three core competencies for AI-era education: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It draws on a conceptual discussion, informal discussions at a Swiss university of applied sciences, and a narrative literature review, then illustrates the approach through a case study of Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich. The case describes how the institution created AI guidelines for student work, requiring transparency about tools used, how they were used, and how outputs were critically evaluated. The paper also summarizes examples of classroom uses such as AI experiments, case study generation, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive technologies.

The main conclusion is that simple bans or unrestricted permission are both inadequate. Instead, institutions should build an AI culture through workshops, clear guidelines, ongoing staff support, dedicated resources, and deliberate instruction in AI literacy and prompt engineering. The author emphasizes that students should use AI as a sparring partner rather than a ghostwriter, and that critical reflection is essential to reduce risks such as hallucinations, bias, unethical copying, and diminished learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot for generating and refining text-based responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as one of several AI chatbots/LLMs used by students and lecturers for academic writing, brainstorming, classroom experiments, and prompt-engineering practice; also referenced in the institution's guidelines as an example model.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational large language model chatbot for generating text and other outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned in the institutional guidance as an example of an AI model students might declare using; also referred to via Bard as a comparable chatbot for classroom experimentation.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's conversational large language model chatbot for generating text-based responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Listed in the paper's example disclosure of AI tools that students should document if used in academic work.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbots and related generative models used for text, image, and sound creation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a broad category for AI tools discussed conceptually in higher education and K-12-adjacent classroom practice, including student writing support, case-study generation, curricula support, gamification, immersive/virtual reality, and prompt-engineering pedagogy.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review with a single institutional case example, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. No controlled study, sample-based outcome data, or tool-specific effect estimates are reported.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for meaningful educational relevance and identifies practical risks and limitations, but it does not report measured impacts or effect sizes. As a framework paper, its influence is conceptual rather than evidence-quantified.
